content: The measurement of a patient’s body temperature is a fundamental component of a comprehensive clinical examination. The core body temperature is tightly regulated within a narrow range to ensure the proper functioning of essential enzymatic reactions. Sustained elevations in temperature (hyperthermia) or depressions (hypothermia) are incompatible with life. There are natural fluctuations in body temperature depending on the time of day and physiological conditions. Rectal temperatures are typically 0.6°F to 0.9°F higher than oral temperatures, while axillary (armpit) temperatures are generally lower by a similar margin. Oral temperature is measured by placing a thermometer under the tongue for 3 to 5 minutes. A temperature above 38°C (100°F) is classified as a fever. It is important to note that consuming hot or cold beverages can affect the accuracy of oral temperature readings for up to 30 minutes. Methods of Temperature Measurement Direct measurement of core body temperature requires invasive techniques, such as the insertion of a probe, which is not feasible in routine clinical practice. Therefore, various indirect methods are employed. Rectal temperature measurement is considered the most accurate reflection of core body temperature, but it is often disliked by both patients and healthcare providers. Additionally, there is a risk of injury if excessive force is applied to hold traditional glass thermometers in place, as they may break, releasing toxic mercury or alcohol. This risk has been mitigated by the use of electronic thermometers, which are constructed from solid plastic and utilize a thermocouple sensor for measurement. Plastic thermometer strips that change color when placed on the forehead provide an approximate local temperature reading. However, these readings are significantly influenced by ambient air temperature and local blood circulation. Axillary temperature measurement is less affected by surrounding air temperature but may still deviate from true core body temperature, particularly in cases of altered blood flow. Recently, small ear thermometers have gained popularity. These devices measure the infrared heat emitted by the tympanic membrane (eardrum), which closely reflects core body temperature. They provide rapid readings, often within one second, making them especially useful for pediatric patients. Historically, rectal temperature measurement was the preferred method for patients unable to hold a thermometer in their mouth, and it remains the gold standard, particularly in cases of hypothermia. Problems with Various Measurement Methods It is argued that changes in core body temperature are detected more quickly and accurately in the ear than at other sites. While the digital display of ear thermometers is easier to interpret than the graduated markings on traditional thermometers, concerns remain about their accuracy in home settings. Factors influencing temperature readings at different sites include: Oral temperatures: These can be affected by recent eating, drinking, or breathing patterns. Rectal temperatures: These may lag behind actual changes in core body temperature and carry a risk of cross-contamination. Skin temperatures: Measurements taken under the arm or on the forehead are not always reliable indicators of core body temperature, particularly during critical periods when core temperature is rising or falling. This is because the skin plays a role in thermoregulation. For instance, during the onset of fever, individuals may shiver and retain heat to elevate their core temperature. Conversely, skin temperature can be influenced by factors such as antipyretic medications, clothing, and external environmental conditions.
